E0496.summary: An initiate whose account, cited from Apuleius's Metamorphoses Book 11, Atwood uses to illustrate what was done in the Mysteries.
E0496.body: Atwood cites, from Apuleius, *Metam.* Book 11, the Epidaurian's first-person account as an initiate's report of what was done in the Mysteries (quoted voice): “I approached the confines of death, and, having trod the threshold of Proserpine, I returned from it” [II.3 ¶45; II.3 n49].

E0497.summary: A work quoted from its end in support of the claim that the all-begetting Spirit dwells within us.
E0497.body: Cited from the end of the *Epistle to Trithemius* (quoted voice) in support of the view, which Atwood adopts, that the all-begetting Spirit dwells in us: “But the Spirit begetting all doth in us dwell” [II.1 ¶27; II.1 n27].

E0498.summary: The final grade of initiation, following telete and muesis, in which initiates are fixed as spectators of the intelligible and shown the Universal Nature and the soul.
E0498.body: In Atwood's account (ATWOOD voice), epopteia is the last of three grades of initiation: “For telete precedes muesis, and muesis, epopteia” [II.4 ¶23]. The record describes it as being fixed as spectators of the intelligible, its content being the revelation of the Universal Nature and of the soul [II.4 ¶23].

E0499.summary: In Khunrath's words, the Stone's balancing power by which it drives out suffering and disease of mind and body.
E0499.body: Quoted from Khunrath: the Stone “by its own equilibriate virtue expels suffering and every disease whether of mind or body” [IV.3 ¶28]. The context suggests a link with the health described nearby, from Julian, as a symmetry or equilibrium of nature [IV.3 ¶30]; the connection is the reader's comparison, not stated outright.

E0500.summary: Cited for his burlesques, which Atwood uses to illustrate the alchemical mania of the age.
E0500.body: Atwood mentions Erasmus's burlesques as illustrating the alchemical mania of the age [I.1 ¶64].

E0501.summary: In the passage given by the metropolitan of Memphis, Eros is born at the same birth as Hyle and called chief of the Immortals.
E0501.body: In the passage quoted from the metropolitan of Memphis (quoted voice), Eros is born at the same birth as Hyle: “the amiable Eros, chief of the Immortals” [III.3 ¶46].

E0502.summary: Book of Esdras, cited to show that few attain the work and for the 'outgoings of paradise', identified with the seven mystic mountains.
E0502.body: Atwood quotes Esdras (Book 1, cap. 3) to illustrate that few attain the work: “The earth giveth much mould, whereof earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold cometh of” [II.2 ¶29; II.2 n20]. She also cites Esdras for the 'outgoings of paradise', which are identified with the seven mystic mountains [II.4 ¶9].

E0503.summary: In Eirenaeus, what gold and Mercury are recongealed into, healing all griefs; in Aristotle and Porphyry, separate particular subsistence and one's own Essence to be established in.
E0503.body:
The word appears in quoted voices with different senses.

- **Eirenaeus**: gold and Mercury are recongealed “Both to an Essence which all griefs canheal.” [III.1 ¶69].
- **Aristotle** (as quoted): “a separate subsistence as this or that particular thing especially belongs to what we call essence, (that is to say, composition of subject and object is necessarily implied in the idea of true intelligence)” [III.2 ¶53]; in this passage Matter is not essence [III.2 ¶53].
- **Porphyry**: the reader is to be “being established in yourself and in your own Essence” [III.2 ¶59].

These uses are not reconciled in the records.

E0504.summary: What the Stone is made manifest as; identified with the true Form or Idea of Gold (Appendix).
E0504.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says the Stone is made manifest as an Essence of Light, “which Essence is the true Form or Idea of Gold” [APP ¶6].

E0505.summary: In the Aristotle passage, the intellect to which human reason is subordinate.
E0505.body: Quoted from Aristotle: human reason is described as subordinate “on account of its subordination to essential intellect” [II.1 ¶34].

E0506.summary: In Porphyry, an essence infinite in power, self-established and self-sufficient, to which nothing can be added and which place or relation would diminish.
E0506.body: Atwood quotes Porphyry (spelled here “Prophyry”): “When you have assumed to yourself an Eternal Essence, says Prophyry, infinite in itself according to power” [III.2 ¶59]. Such an essence is self-established and self-sufficient, seeking nothing but itself; nothing can be added to it, and adding place or relation diminishes it; “it is much more sufficient than any perpetually flowing fountain can be conceived to be” [III.2 ¶59].

E0507.summary: In the theosophist's account, Adam's leader, which had dominion in him in his Paradisiacal innocency.
E0507.body: Quoted from the theosophist: in Adam's Paradisiacal innocency “The Eternal Word was his leader, and had dominion in him” [IV.3 ¶38].

E0508.summary: Atwood's universal subtle medium: an all-pervading perfective essence, vehicle of the world-soul, which, separated and purified, is the matter of the Stone and rises into Light.
E0508.body:
**Nature and authorities.** With Homberg, Boerhaave, Boyle and Berkeley, Atwood describes Ether as a distinct, universally diffused substance, sensible only in its mixtures and effects, source and bond of the elements, giving air its vitalizing power: “the occult virtues of the Ether; its all-pervading essence and perfective power” [I.2 ¶12]; one authority calls it “ether, and a pure invisible fire” [I.2 ¶14]. The **Free Ether** (voice of the Greeks) is “freed from the prison of gross matter, and able to work of itself intimately by the virtue of its own included light” [I.2 ¶16]; Euripides calls it Jove: “The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove” [I.2 ¶17]. Ovid's verse gives “liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera, non quicquam terrenae faecis habentum” (ours: liquid and weightless ether, having nothing of earthly dregs) [III.2 ¶37].

**In the Art (ATWOOD).** Separated and purified it is the matter of the Stone: “the Formal Light, by multiplication in its Ethe, is said to produce gold” [I.2 ¶46]; the Stone has “its foundation in the free Ether” [IV.4 ¶2]. Alchemists are “our Oedipus distillers of this Ether” [III.1 ¶13], ending in “the final resurrection of the pure Ether into Light” [III.1 ¶21], “depriving the ether of its wild affections and impressures” [IV.1 ¶4]. Pseudo-alchemists tried “to compress and entice the ether by mangetical disposition” and failed [II.1 ¶6]. Asserted identities: the alchemists' mineral tree [II.3 ¶18]; “that Augean palace” of the multiplied Prester [II.3 ¶56]; “the Sphinx of the Universe” [III.1 ¶5]; non-being, the “simple Understanding of its ether” [III.3 ¶15].

**In man and cosmos.** “what the natural intelligent Spirit is in man, that Ether is in the universe” [III.1 ¶5], vehicle of the world-soul. Wholeness comes “from equilibriate circulation in their Ether” [II.4 ¶29]; rites work “by the medium of the passive Ether” [II.4 ¶36]; Intellect rides “secure in its Ether” [IV.1 ¶33]; see also “the liquid crystal of the understanding ether” [III.3 ¶10]. Imaginations can “pollute the ether of their pertinacious abode” [III.4 ¶42]; ether also names the anaesthetic [IV.1 ¶4]. In Boehme the Tincture “stays in its ether” [III.2 ¶16]; in Khunrath's source (voice unclear) ether in the divine water “will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20].

**Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, later layer).** “The Ether is two-fold: the mundane, which is full of the false forms; the pure, which is not of this world” [APP ¶64]; it is “a quintessence of those very four principles” and “the Quintessence of both worlds” [APP ¶69]; each has “a scrap of that ether shut in at our birth-conception”, “the omnia in omnibus of the Hermetic Riddle” [APP ¶119]; the spirit-man's work “is to move the Ether” [APP ¶139]; of Lucifer, ether is identified with Heaven: “burn up the ether which was Heaven.” [APP ¶133]; “The Ether is the universal extended Matter; the Divine posit everywhere; life.” [APP ¶179].

E0509.summary: In the Appendix, the first Ether arising from nature, through which thoughts, images, passions and desires rise to their own sphere, beneath the pure Ether and the Divine Light.
E0509.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860, a later layer), Atwood says thoughts, images, passions and desires “all rise up through this first Ether Natural and abide on a sphere of their own above it” [APP ¶170]. Above it lies the pure Ether, related to the moral nature, and then the region of Divine Light [APP ¶170].

E0510.summary: The ethereal which art separates from mortal existence, read as Plato's One Whole and Aristotle's perfect world; its estates rise successively, figured in Hesiod's generations.
E0510.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) reads Plato and Aristotle as pointing to it: “Plato yet more plainly alluding to the Etheral Quintessence, in Timaeus, says, that of four elements the Demiurgus assumed One Whole from wholes” — perfect and free from age and disease; of such descriptions she asks “what other, therefore, should they either mean but the ethereal” [III.2 ¶38]. In the plural, the Ethereal Quintessences are successive estates called forth by the light and heat of the superincumbent mind: “the several estates of the Ethereal Quintessences arising one above another”, figured in Hesiod's generations [III.3 ¶42].

E0511.summary: The one being whose relation, action and passion the authors mean by sulfur, mercury, earth, and twofold or third matter.
E0511.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) says the authors' various names (sulfur, mercury, earth, twofold or third matter) refer to “the magnetic relation, action, and passion of the Ethereal being in itself” [I.2 ¶42].

E0512.summary: The subject described by negations (no form, quality, body, reason or bound, but a certain Infinity) in Atwood's discussion of Matter.
E0512.body: Continuing her discussion of Matter, Atwood writes: “But since the ethereal element is described by so many ablative characteristics” [III.2 ¶53], namely that it is neither form, quality, body, reason nor bound, but a certain Infinity. The text does not state that the ethereal element is the same as Matter, though the context suggests a close link.

E0513.summary: Something passive to intellect as a mirror is to images, subsisting without imagination, felt rather than known; the Passive Nature is said to be of this kind.
E0513.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) compares it to a mirror: “so is this ethereal glass to intellect, subsisting according to processure and in defect of all imagination” [III.2 ¶60]. It is felt, not known, and the Passive Nature is said to be a thing of this kind [III.2 ¶60].

E0514.summary: The moisture that nourishes and educates the Solar Light, set beside Luna as 'Domina Humiditatis'.
E0514.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): “The ethereal humidity nourishes the Solar Light and educates it” [IV.1 ¶29]; it is set beside Luna, called Domina Humiditatis (ours: mistress of moisture) [IV.1 ¶29].

E0515.summary: The Greek counterpart of the alchemists' first matter: the one life-substance divided into three principles in dissolution, which revolves in its First Cause when the Stone is confirmed.
E0515.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice) treats it as the Greek counterpart of the alchemists' first matter: “that ethereal hypostasis we were before discussing” [III.1 ¶3]. In the dissolution, “the ethereal hypostasis is divided against itself and brought to a separation even as these three” principles [III.1 ¶53]. When the Stone is confirmed, rising in rational supremacy over sense and finite reflection, “the Ethereal Hypostasis revolves in its First Cause” [IV.3 ¶62]; that passage does not define it further. See also “filling the Ethereal Hypostasis with acme and power” [II.4 ¶29].

E0516.summary: That which, in the Fifth Essence, becomes a Circle of golden light in eternity.
E0516.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): in the Fifth Essence “the Ethereal Quadrangle becomes a Circle of golden light in eternity” [III.3 ¶32].

E0517.summary: The sought spirit, never existing separately on earth but hidden in the beings it sustains; in Synesius, the intermediate nature joining divine and lowest, phantastic until purified by art.
E0517.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): “the ethereal spirit does not subsist of itself, separate or tangibly on earth” [I.2 ¶20], but is hidden and defiled within the beings it sustains. She equates its subjugation with that of the Sphinx: the trial “ends in her subjugation; in other words, the Ethereal Spirit abandons her phantasy” [III.1 ¶20], yielding the clear light of understanding to the trained investigator. Quoting Synesius, it is the intermediate nature between rational and brutal life, corporeal and incorporeal: “it is the medium which conjoins divine natures with the lowest of all” [II.2 ¶10]. It is identified with “the phantastical condition also of the natural understanding essence, before it is purified by art and exalted. This Etherial Spirit” [II.2 ¶10].

E0518.summary: The prepared medium in which the seed of gold is planted so as to bring forth its virtue in manifold increase.
E0518.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): the seed of gold must be “planted in its proper ethereal vehicle, well prepared and fallow” to bring forth its virtue in manifold increase [I.3 n40]. Elsewhere the divine unions “tried the ethereal vehicle to its utmost susceptibility” [II.4 ¶40].

E0519.summary: The waters on which the displaced sulfur floats while they tear, decoct and soften the sensual dominant.
E0519.body: Atwood (ATWOOD voice): the displaced sulfur is made “to float upon the ethereal waters, whilst these continue to tear, decoct, and soften the sensual dominant” [III.1 ¶53].

E0520.summary: A work cited for Tartarus as the region next beyond Hades.
E0520.body: Cited for Tartarus as the next region beyond Hades [II.3 ¶36].

E0521.summary: Used in contrast to Christian; not further defined.
E0521.body: Used by Atwood in contrast to Christian, “both Ethnic and Christian” [II.2 ¶5]; the text does not define it further.

E0522.summary: A group whose Anima Mundi doctrine Atwood says agrees in substance with Hebrew doctrine.
E0522.body: Atwood says the Ethnics' doctrine of the Anima Mundi agrees in substance with Hebrew doctrine [I.2 ¶14].

E0523.summary: Speaker of The Six Keys of Eudoxus, which Atwood quotes as practical instruction on the Art until its defective final Keys make her turn elsewhere.
E0523.body: Atwood cites Eudoxus's introduction to the Six Keys in support of the view that the difficulty lies in learning the Art from books and that the seeker needs deep knowledge of Nature: “the practice of our Art is the most difficult thing in the world, not in regard to its operation” [IV.2 ¶4]. *The Six Keys of Eudoxus, Opening Into the Most Secret Philosophy* is named in a chapter heading [IV.3 ¶1], which makes him the first-person speaker of the quoted text that follows; Atwood presents it as instruction on the practice [IV.3 ¶10; IV.3 ¶12; IV.3 ¶14; IV.3 ¶16]. She qualifies its usefulness: its last Keys, on Multiplication and Projection, are avowedly defective, “The Keys of Eudoxus open no more” [IV.3 ¶17], so she turns to another source.

E0524.summary: Eudoxus as reported in Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride, cited for the myth of Jupiter's grown-together feet freed by Isis, which Atwood reads as an allegory of the Art.
E0524.body: Atwood cites Eudoxus in Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride*, for the myth in which Isis frees Jupiter's grown-together feet; she reads it as an allegory of the Art. The interpretation quoted: “the mind and reason of the Supreme God, which in nature is invisible and dwelling in obscurity, by being put in motion becomes known” [III.1 ¶23; III.1 n28].

E0525.summary: Quoted for Ether called Jove, for the felicity of seeing the Mysteries, and from the Bacchis on death, purification and initiation.
E0525.body: Atwood quotes Euripides (quoted voice) in support of her account of Ether as all-nourishing and called Jove: “The viewless Ether in his genial arms Clasping the earth; Him call thou Lord and Jove” [I.2 ¶17; I.2 n16]. To show that the people placed their chief felicity in the Mysteries, she quotes a line spoken by Hercules and one from the *Bacchis*: “I was blessed when I got a sight of the mysteries” [II.2 ¶5; II.2 n8]. From *Bacchis* she also takes “a dream of death” for the threshold where the Lesser Mysteries end [II.3 ¶36; II.3 n48], and Bacchae verses supporting purification and initiation [II.3 ¶43; II.3 ¶44].
